121.event_title: Stanislav Petrov judges a missile alert to be false
121.place: Early-warning command bunker near Moscow, Soviet Union (now Russia)
121.event: Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov was on duty at a Soviet early-warning bunker outside Moscow when the satellite system reported that the United States had launched five intercontinental ballistic missiles at the Soviet Union. Reasoning that a real American first strike would use far more than five missiles, and with ground radars not confirming the launches, he reported the alert as a false alarm rather than treating it as an attack; the satellites had mistaken sunlight reflecting off clouds for missile launches. He was reprimanded over paperwork rather than rewarded, the incident stayed secret until after the Soviet Union collapsed, and he later received international honours including the 2013 Dresden Peace Prize, although Russia's UN mission argued that no single officer could have started or prevented a nuclear war.
121.explanation: In a period of high tension, one officer's refusal to act on alarm rather than evidence is widely credited with avoiding a possible catastrophe.
121.tie_back: The kural sets restraint, which raises a person among the immortals, against its absence, which leads into thick darkness; Petrov's restraint is remembered worldwide, while the alternative could have meant darkness for millions.
121._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of restraint under pressure, but the kural's restraint is a lifelong moral discipline rather than a single professional judgment.

122.event: On 10 April 1838 the Capuchin priest Theobald Mathew presided at the first meeting of the Cork Total Abstinence Society in his own schoolhouse and took the pledge of total abstinence himself. Between 1838 and 1842 he travelled throughout Ireland, where whole crowds took the pledge, and by 1841 the number of abstainers in Ireland was estimated at 4,647,000. Britannica records that within three years consumption of spirits fell by about half, much of the decrease being attributed to his efforts.
122.explanation: Millions treated a vow of self-restraint as something worth guarding, and contemporaries credited the movement with improvements in public order, though historians note that its gains were weakened by the Great Famine.
122.tie_back: The kural says to guard self-restraint like a treasure, since no living being has a greater good; the pledge movement asked ordinary people to do exactly that.
122._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for restraint valued as a social good, but it concerns one kind of restraint (from alcohol) and many pledges were not kept for life.

123.event_title: Albert Luthuli receives the Nobel Peace Prize
123.place: Groutville, South Africa, and Oslo, Norway
123.event: Albert Luthuli, a teacher and chief who was elected president-general of the African National Congress in December 1952, became the spokesman of a campaign of nonviolent civil disobedience against South Africa's racial segregation laws, inspired by Gandhi's philosophy. He was dismissed as chief, repeatedly banned and confined to his rural district, and arrested in the treason arrests of 1956, yet he continued to appeal for nonviolence and a shared society. The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded him the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent struggle against apartheid, making him Africa's first Peace Prize laureate; he received it the following year.
123.explanation: Luthuli's disciplined refusal to meet persecution with violence was recognised by the wider world even while his own government silenced him.
123.tie_back: The kural says that restraint understood as wisdom and practised rightly will be recognised by the good and bring distinction; Luthuli's restraint earned the world's highest honour for peace.
123._accuracy_note: A strong fit for restraint recognised by others; historians still debate Luthuli's attitude to the ANC's later turn to armed struggle.

124.place: Maryland State House, Annapolis, Maryland, United States
124.event: After British troops evacuated New York at the end of the American Revolutionary War, General George Washington, commander-in-chief of the Continental Army, bade farewell to his officers and travelled to Annapolis, where the Continental Congress was meeting. On 23 December 1783, in the Senate chamber of the Maryland State House, he resigned his commission before Congress in an emotional ceremony. He left Annapolis at dawn the next day and reached his home at Mount Vernon on Christmas Eve, a private citizen for the first time in almost nine years.
124.explanation: At the height of his power and popularity, Washington handed military authority back to the civilian government and returned to private life.
124.tie_back: The kural says the stature of one who stays restrained and does not swerve from his proper path rises higher than a mountain; Washington's voluntary return to private life is still commemorated in the room where it happened.
124._accuracy_note: A strong fit for restraint that enlarged a person's stature, though the kural speaks of the householder's ordinary path rather than political power.

125.event_title: Princess Elizabeth trains as an army mechanic
125.place: Auxiliary Territorial Service training centre, southern England, United Kingdom
125.event: Princess Elizabeth, heir to the British throne, turned 18 in April 1944, and in February 1945 she enlisted in the Auxiliary Territorial Service, the women's branch of the British Army, as Second Subaltern Elizabeth Alexandra Mary Windsor. On a driving and vehicle maintenance course she learned to service, maintain and drive heavy army vehicles, and the Imperial War Museums notes that she was treated the same as the rest of her company. She became the first woman in the Royal Family to be a full-time member of the armed services and qualified as a driver before the war ended.
125.explanation: The press nicknamed her Princess Auto Mechanic, and her willingness to do ordinary work alongside other young women was widely admired.
125.tie_back: The kural says humility is good in everyone but shines like a second wealth in the wealthy; a future queen in overalls changing tyres displayed exactly that kind of humility.
125._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for humility in one born to great wealth and rank, though the sources describe her service rather than her personal motives in detail.

126.event_title: Gandhi's three vows before sailing to England
126.event: When the 18-year-old Mohandas Gandhi prepared to leave Rajkot to study law in England in 1888, his mother feared that young men there took to meat and liquor and hesitated to let him go. Becharji Swami, a Jain monk and family adviser, administered a solemn oath in which Gandhi vowed to abstain from wine, women and meat, and only then did his mother give her permission. Gandhi recounted the episode in his autobiography, The Story of My Experiments with Truth.
126.explanation: Gandhi later treated keeping these vows as an early discipline of his life, and self-restraint of the senses became central to his ideas.
126.tie_back: The kural praises drawing in the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs; Gandhi's three vows were a deliberate withdrawal from the pleasures his mother feared would capture him abroad.
126._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for sense restraint undertaken as a vow; the kural's image covers all five senses, while the vows addressed three specific temptations.

127.event_title: Kaiser Wilhelm II and the Daily Telegraph interview
127.place: London, United Kingdom, and Berlin, Germany
127.event: On 28 October 1908 the London Daily Telegraph published an account of conversations in which Kaiser Wilhelm II spoke with what the paper called impulsive and unusual frankness, telling the English they were mad as March hares and saying that much of his own people was unfriendly to England. The remarks angered the British public, were seen in France and Russia as a diplomatic blunder, and set off a political crisis in Germany: in the Reichstag debate of 10 and 11 November all parties criticised the Kaiser, who considered abdicating, and Chancellor Bernhard von Bulow demanded that he change his behaviour. German History in Documents notes that the affair discredited him in the eyes of many Germans and ultimately weakened his position.
127.explanation: An emperor's unguarded talk, meant to improve relations, instead offended three foreign nations and his own parliament at once.
127.tie_back: The kural says that whatever else you fail to guard, guard your tongue, for those who do not will grieve; the Kaiser's careless words brought him exactly that grief.
127._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the cost of an unguarded tongue, with consequences that fell on the speaker himself.

128.event_title: Gerald Ratner's speech destroys his company's reputation
128.place: Institute of Directors convention, London, England, United Kingdom
128.event: Gerald Ratner had built Ratners Group into Britain's biggest jewellery chain by selling inexpensive jewellery to a mass market. Speaking at the Institute of Directors' convention in London in April 1991, he joked that one of his firm's products was so cheap because it was rubbish, using a crude word, and that a pair of its earrings would probably not last as long as a prawn sandwich. The remarks were widely reported, the value of the group fell by around 500 million pounds, nearly causing its collapse, and Ratner was removed as chief executive the following year.
128.explanation: Years of commercial success were undone in a few seconds, and doing a Ratner became a British phrase for a self-inflicted business blunder.
128.tie_back: The kural says that if even a single harmful word does its damage, all the good a person has done turns to no good; Ratner's few words wiped out the reputation he had spent years building.
128._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of one harmful remark cancelling a record of achievement, though the harm was commercial rather than moral.

129.event_title: Lincoln's unsent letter to General Meade
129.place: Executive Mansion (White House), Washington, D.C., United States
129.event: After the Union victory at Gettysburg, Confederate General Robert E. Lee's army escaped back across the Potomac River, and General George Meade, stung by word of the president's disappointment, asked to be relieved of his command. On 14 July 1863 Abraham Lincoln wrote Meade a letter thanking him for Gettysburg but sharply criticising him for letting Lee escape, calling the lost chance a misfortune that would prolong the war. Lincoln never sent it; he placed the letter in an envelope on which he wrote that it was to Gen. Meade, never sent, or signed.
129.explanation: Lincoln put his anger into words on paper but kept those words from wounding a general he still needed, a habit the American Battlefield Trust describes as one of his favourite coping mechanisms.
129.tie_back: The kural says a burn from fire heals but a wound from the tongue never does; by holding back a cutting letter, Lincoln avoided inflicting a wound that could not be undone.
129._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the kural from the side of prevention: it shows harsh words withheld rather than a lasting wound actually inflicted.

130.event_title: Abdul Ghaffar Khan and the nonviolent Servants of God
130.place: North-West Frontier Province, British India (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
130.event: Abdul Ghaffar Khan, a Pashtun reformer from near Peshawar who founded schools to spread education, established the Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God) movement, dated by The Tribune to 1929, an unarmed volunteer force of tens of thousands that resisted British rule through civil disobedience. On joining, members swore to forgive anyone who oppressed or mistreated them, to lead a simple life and to perform social service for at least two hours a day. Repeatedly imprisoned by both British and Pakistani governments, he was honoured by India in 1987 as the first non-Indian recipient of its highest civilian award, the Bharat Ratna.
130.explanation: Khan asked people from a region with strong traditions of armed revenge to master their anger, and his steadfast restraint brought him honour in several countries in his own lifetime.
130.tie_back: The kural says virtue itself waits on the path of one who guards against anger, is learned and is capable of restraint; recognition sought out Abdul Ghaffar Khan rather than the other way round.
130._accuracy_note: A strong fit for mastery of anger joined to learning and restraint; the kural's image of virtue waiting on a person's path can only be illustrated loosely by later honours.
